Matthias of Janov
ma-thi'as of ya'nov
n. (Matthias of Janov, c. 1350–1393, master of Paris, Prague preacher, author of the Rules of the Old and New Testament)
Janov, a Bohemian place-name, a village of John; Matthias, from Hebrew Mattithyah, gift of the LORD.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Matthias of Janov was a Bohemian priest who took his master's degree at Paris, served as a canon at Prague, and spent his last years writing the long work called the Rules of the Old and New Testament. It is the most important book written in Bohemia before Hus and it contains, twenty years early, most of what the Hussite movement would afterwards fight about. Its governing idea is that Scripture is the rule by which everything in the church is to be measured, and that what cannot be measured by it has been added. By that rule he condemned the multiplication of images, the traffic in relics, the invocation of saints, pilgrimages and the swollen apparatus of ceremonies, calling them a crust grown over the simple thing Christ instituted; he urged the frequent communion of the laity as the proper remedy for a cold church; and he described the corrupted hierarchy of his own day under the name of the mystical body of Antichrist, by which he meant not one man but a system that had taken Christ's place in the church. He was made to recant some of this in 1389 and submitted. He died in 1393, two years before Hus began to preach at Bethlehem chapel. The dictionary enters him because the Bohemian Reformation did not begin with a political quarrel; it began with a man applying a rule.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a rule as that which is prescribed as a guide; a relic as the remains of a saint preserved as an object of veneration; and Antichrist as one who opposes Christ, or usurps his place.

expand to see more

RULE, n. [L. regula.] That which is prescribed or laid down as a guide to conduct; a standard to which to conform, or by which to judge.

RELIC, n. [L. reliquiae.] That which remains; the remains of the body of a saint, or of something belonging to him, preserved as an object of veneration.

ANTICHRIST, n. A great adversary of Christ; the man of sin; one who opposes Christ, or usurps his authority and place in the church.

CEREMONY, n. [L. caeremonia.] Outward rite; external form in religion; forms of civility; outward forms of state.

COMMUNION, n. [L. communio.] Fellowship; the act of partaking of the Lord's supper; mutual intercourse or union.

Key Scripture

Isa 8:20 — "To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them."

Mat 7:15 — "Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves."

Exo 20:4 — "Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth:"

1Co 11:26 — "For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord's death till he come."

Modern Corruption

Prague writer whose Rules of the Old and New Testament set Scripture as the measure of the church twenty years before Hus preached.

expand to see more

The corruption he named is the overgrowth: a church which had not denied the gospel in words but had buried it under additions, each of which had once been a devotion and had become a law. Images, relics, pilgrimages and the invocation of saints are the particulars; the principle is that whatever the church adds to what Christ instituted will in time be required, and what Christ instituted will in time be neglected. His own evidence was the plainest possible: a people kept from the cup at the Supper while the shrines of the city did a profitable trade.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the rule itself. “To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20) is a rule of measurement, and the Reformation's great recovery was not a new doctrine but the courage to apply it to the church's own practice. Matthias applied it, was made to recant in 1389, and submitted; the dictionary records the submission as a failure and the rule as the thing that outlived him.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew torah (H8451), law or instruction; Greek kanon (G2583), a measuring rod, a rule.

expand to see more

Hebrew torah (H8451) — law, instruction, direction; “To the law and to the testimony”, Isaiah 8:20.

Hebrew te'udah (H8584) — testimony, attestation; Isaiah 8:20.

Greek pseudoprophetes (G5578) — a false prophet; “Beware of false prophets”, Matthew 7:15.

Hebrew pesel (H6459) — a graven image; “any graven image, or any likeness”, Exodus 20:4.

Greek katangello (G2605) — to proclaim, to shew forth; “ye do shew the Lord's death till he come”, 1 Corinthians 11:26.

Usage

"“To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20) — the governing rule of his Rules of the Old and New Testament."

"“Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image” (Exo 20:4) — against the multiplication of images and the traffic in relics."

"“For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup” (1Co 11:26) — his plea for the frequent communion of the laity."
